name: SLOs and Error Budgets
intent: Turn 'the service should be reliable' into a number you measure and a budget you can spend, so teams can decide objectively between shipping features and fixing reliability.
scenario: The product team wants to ship weekly. The operations team wants fewer outages. Both are right, and without a shared number every discussion becomes an argument about opinions.
problem: Perfect reliability is impossible and extremely expensive, and nobody agrees how reliable 'reliable enough' is. Without a target, teams either over-invest in uptime users do not notice or under-invest until customers leave. Alerts based on guesses either miss problems or page people all night.

howItWorks.title: Choose what users care about: the SLI
howItWorks.text: A service level indicator is a measured ratio of good events to total events: the share of requests that succeed, or that complete in under 300 ms. Pick indicators that reflect the user's experience, such as availability and latency of key journeys, not internal numbers like CPU use.

howItWorks.title: Set a target: the SLO
howItWorks.text: A service level objective is the target for the SLI over a window, for example 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days. Pick it from what users need and what you can afford, not from what the system happens to do today. Each extra nine costs far more than the one before.

howItWorks.title: The error budget is what is left over
howItWorks.text: A 99.9% objective allows 0.1% of requests to fail, which is about 43 minutes of full outage per 30 days. That allowance is the error budget. Bad deploys, outages and slow days all spend it. When there is budget left, you can take risks and ship fast.

howItWorks.title: Agree what happens when the budget runs out
howItWorks.text: A written policy decides it: when the budget is spent, feature releases pause and the team works on reliability until the service is back within its objective. This turns a vague argument into a rule that product and engineering agreed to beforehand.

howItWorks.title: Alert on burn rate, not on single blips
howItWorks.text: The burn rate is how fast you are spending budget compared with an even spend. Alert when the budget is being consumed quickly (for example 14 times faster than allowed over one hour) and open a ticket for slow burns. This catches real problems and ignores brief noise.

pros: A shared, measurable definition of 'reliable enough'
Balances reliability work against feature work with data, not opinion
Stops over-engineering: 100% is not the goal
Gives alerting a principled basis (burn rate)
cons: Choosing good SLIs and targets takes real effort and revision
Needs trustworthy measurement, preferably at the user's edge
A budget policy only works if leadership honours it
An SLO met on average can hide a bad experience for a particular group of users
whenToUse: Any user-facing service, and internal services other teams depend on
When you debate reliability against speed of delivery
As the basis for alerts and on-call load
whenNotToUse: A prototype with no real users, where measuring is premature
As a contract with customers: that is an SLA, which has penalties and should be looser than the internal SLO
pitfalls: Setting 99.99% because it sounds good, then ignoring misses
Measuring server health instead of what users experience
Having an SLO but no policy for what to do when it is missed
Alerting on every error instead of on the rate at which the budget is spent

roles.label: Users
roles.description: Experience the service and define what 'good' means.

roles.label: Engineering team
roles.description: Ships changes and spends the budget.

roles.label: Monitoring
roles.description: Measures the SLI and tracks the budget.
